text_results.content: The spread of COVID‐19 and the lockdown policies have led to various economic, social and health consequences, drawing popular and scholarly attention. Recent research has documented the impact of the pandemic on work life, economic conditions (Béland et al., [2020]()), mental health (Brodeur et al., [2021]()) and domestic violence (Leslie & Wilson, [2020]()). These dramatic changes in economic and family lives would create discrepancies between households' needs and their current housing and community environments. However, little research has been done on whether people consider residential moves as an adaptation to the changes caused by the pandemic. A study in Spain reported that approximately 10% of the population moved during the lockdown and analysed the triggers and motivations of these moves (Duque‐Calvache et al., [2020]()), but this study did not compare mobility intentions or behaviours before and after the COVID‐19 outbreak. To fill the gap in the literature, we examine how mobility intentions have changed before and during the COVID‐19 pandemic in the United States.

Out of the 254 (unweighted) respondents in June 2020 (Wave 68) who moved because of COVID, 123 (unweighted) also participated in the survey conducted in November of that year (Wave 79).[Footnote 6]() Approximately one-third of the latter were still living away from their pre-pandemic home but in the same-community, close to one-fourth returned to their initial address, and another 42 percent continued to live in a different community (Table [2](), lower panel). It is likely that COVID migrants chose where to relocate and whether to return or not on the basis, _inter alia,_ of the reason for which they moved e.g., avoiding getting the virus, to be with family, or for educational, economic, and other considerations. More generally, each of the three dimensions—moving or not moving due to the pandemic, the specific coronavirus-related motive for moving, and type of migration—was likely affected by respondents’ demographic and socioeconomic characteristics and/or area-contextual factors. The multivariate analyses that follow provide insights into the direction and strength of these associations and the robustness of the models, namely, how much of the variance they are able to explain.

The COVID‐19 pandemic has disrupted people's lives through economic challenges, closure of worksites and schools and increased health risks. These disruptions can trigger new residential needs and preferences, but little research has been done regarding the impact of the COVID‐19 pandemic on moving intentions. We theorized how the pandemic could influence intentions of making different types of residential moves. Using Google Trends data, we conducted a time‐series analysis to assess the transitory, short‐term and long‐lasting changes in various types of mobility intentions since the pandemic. Results show that thoughts about temporary relocation surged at the onset of the COVID‐19 epidemic and then experienced a long‐term decrease. Intentions to move through housing purchases and rentals briefly declined at the beginning of the pandemic but then surpassed their normal levels in the following months. Thoughts about moving in with family or parents increased by almost 50% during the pandemic. These trends were also reflected in Google searches for moving services, which exhibited an initial decline followed by a long‐term increase. The results demonstrate that the COVID‐19 pandemic has not only posed obstacles that lowered moving intentions but also has created new needs and desires for moving.

As an unanticipated major event, the COVID-19 outbreak was a natural experiment. Relocations in the pre-pandemic stage happened without its influence, while relocations in the post-pandemic stage are subject to its influence. Therefore, with an appropriate method, it is possible to single out its effects on jobs–housing relocation. We adopted an event study approach to compare relocation patterns of relocators from before the pandemic and at different stages after the pandemic. We divided the period between Apr. 2018 and Nov. 2022 into nine semi–annual phases (numbered _j_ = –3, …, 0, …, 5) including three pre–pandemic phases (–3 to –1) and six post-pandemic phases (0 to 5). For each phase, we detected individuals’ home and work locations and focused on relocators—those who had different home locations (home movers), work locations (work movers) or both (home–and–work movers) in the start month and end month. We calculated relocation patterns of relocators from each phase and examined the differences between post–pandemic relocation patterns and pre–pandemic relocation patterns while controlling for pre–relocation jobs–housing characteristics, sociodemographic attributes, and season fixed effects. A diagram of our research design is presented in Fig. [1]().

Third, although the pandemic dampened mobility intentions in the initial stage of the pandemic, since the summer of 2020, it increased searches related to most types of moving, including moves through purchases of houses or condos, house rental and moving in with family. The only exception is moving related to apartment rental. The long‐term increases in searches on purchase‐related and house rental‐related terms reflect a discrepancy between household needs and current residential conditions during the pandemic. For example, working and studying from home may have created demands for larger spaces and better housing conditions. A recent survey showed that the share of Americans who are satisfied with the quality of life in their local community has dropped between 2018 and 2021 (Parker et al., [2021]()). The pandemic could have also changed people's evaluation of place characteristics. Features like high population density and closeness to highways and train/bus stations may be less valued than before. Fewer U.S. adults in 2021 expressed a preference for living in urban areas than in 2018 (Parker et al., [2021]()).

COVID-19 affected the social, economic, and spatial patterns of people’s lives. Families adjusted their places of work, where their children were educated, and their interactions with relatives and friends. The disease weakened some individuals’ and families’ attachment to their places of residence and prompted some to reconsider where to live. We examine the selectivity, reasons, and types of COVID-induced migration in the U.S. during the first year of the pandemic. Using Pew’s American Trends Panel, we find that 3 percent relocated by June 2020 because of the pandemic. One-third of movers feared infection, another quarter wished to be with family, and nearly half were guided by educational and economic considerations. By November, four out of ten were still living outside their origin community, a third dwelled elsewhere in their origin community, and a quarter had returned to their pre-COVID home. Multivariate analyses show that COVID migrants differed from ordinary migrants and from non-movers. High rates of COVID mortality in county of residence heightened the likelihood of moving. Compared with COVID migrants whose concerns were mainly educational and economic, those who feared infection tended to be younger, native-born, non-metro residents, religiously weak, and politically Republican; their counterparts who wished to be close to family were in mid-life, women, college educated, and more likely Republicans. The differences between inter-community migrants and intra-community/return migrants were limited to only a few characteristics i.e., type of residence, educational and economic attainments, and mortality rates in initial county of residence.

Again, we find almost no reference to the pandemic as an immediate trigger for relocating. A few examples refer to job losses or constraints in searching for a new dwelling. In the summer of 2020, working from home was not yet as established as it was one or two years later. Therefore, the following statement provided as a reason for an urban-rural move proves to be an exception: _‘partner with detached house and working there remotely during the coronavirus pandemic led to a change of residence’_ (ID 20170106).

We ran two samples of 1,000 respondents for the same set of questions (noted as survey 1) conducted on 5 May 2020 (57% female; mean age, 43 years; age s.d., 16 years) and 27 August 2020 (55% female; mean age, 42 years; age s.d., 15 years) and a slightly updated version (survey 2) on 19 October 2020 (57% female; mean age, 38 years; age s.d., 13 years). We ran a final survey, also 1,000 respondents (49% female; mean age, 39 years; age s.d., 11 years), on 15 April 2021 (survey 3). The multi-waves were designed to capture the trends in our core questions of sentiment and behaviour as the pandemic progressed. Surveys were conducted within native advertising units in a mix of mobile applications on both iOS and Android, and in both mobile and desktop web experiences, using the Pollfish interface and delivery mechanism. The participants were at least 18 years old, and were randomly selected from the pool of eligible respondents. We asked a total of 25 questions in survey 1 and 18 questions in surveys 2 and 3 (see the [Supplementary Information]() for a full list of questions, including both exploratory questions as well as specific questions to be used in this paper). These survey results were raked to reflect national Census estimates of key demographics.

To conceptualize the COVID-19 pandemic’s influence on relocation, we draw on migration theories including the stress–response model (Wolpert, [1966]( "Wolpert J \(1966\) Migration as an adjustment to environmental stress. Journal of Social Issues 22\(4\):92–102")) and the dissatisfaction model (Speare, [1974]( "Speare A \(1974\) Residential satisfaction as an intervening variable in residential mobility. Demography 11\(2\):173–188")). The stress–response model believes that relocation is triggered by environmental stress in the current location (Wolpert, [1966]( "Wolpert J \(1966\) Migration as an adjustment to environmental stress. Journal of Social Issues 22\(4\):92–102")). The pandemic has introduced many stress factors. In residential areas, due to mobility restrictions, people stay at home longer, making residential areas more crowded, which may inflict neighbourhood tension and also increase infection risks. In workplaces, the most outstanding stress factor is infection risk. The dissatisfaction model believes that relocation is triggered by dissatisfaction with the current location. This theory entertains the thought that when new needs emerges, the current location, once satisfactory, may start to seem dissatisfactory (Speare, [1974]( "Speare A \(1974\) Residential satisfaction as an intervening variable in residential mobility. Demography 11\(2\):173–188")). The pandemic has created new jobs–housing needs and preferences (Lei and Liu, [2022]( "Lei L, Liu X \(2022\) The COVID–19 pandemic and residential mobility intentions in the United States: Evidence from Google Trends data. Population Space and Place 28:e2581")). For example, since the pandemic people have become more aware of health issues and may need more natural amenities near their homes; people who work from home may want to improve their living environment as they will be spending more time at home. In short, COVID-19 may have introduced stress factors in people’s current jobs–housing locations, and may have created new jobs–housing requirement. This “push–pull” situation may lead to jobs–housing relocations.

We focused on the differences between COVID-19 migrants and economic migrants as well as persons who did not change their residence during the early months of the COVID pandemic. We also examined the social and economic attributes that were associated with the primary reasons for pandemic-induced migration; and how migrants differed by distance moved and permanency of their move. To this end, we utilized data from two waves of Pew’s American Trends Panel (ATP). Descriptive results suggest that by early June 2020 just over 3 percent of American adults had left their homes because of the pandemic. Among them, about a third stated that fear of infection was their most important reason for moving, another quarter wished to be with family, and nearly half were guided by the pandemic’s educational and economic implications. Hence, migration associated with the pandemic was often a mixture of both environmental coercion, and economic and social concerns. We followed up a subset of the COVID migrants to see if they remained outside of their original residence five months after moving. This analysis revealed that by November of 2020 four out of ten migrants were still living outside their origin community, about a third were in different home but in their original community, and close to a quarter had returned to their initial address.

Similar to research reviewed outside of the U.S., we also identified only very few studies that examined reasons for migration during COVID although several were concerned with the role of family relationships in channeling spatial movement. Using a large survey of interstate movers during 2018 and 2023, Haslag and Weagley ([2023]( "Haslag, P., & Weagley, D. \(2023\). From L.A. to Boise: How migration has changed during the COVID-19 pandemic. Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis, 2023, 1–31.")) found that concern about COVID was a factor in 12 percent of interstate moves that occurred during this period. Among those whose moves were associated with COVID, some had lost their jobs, hence their move combined both COVID and economic-related motives. Moreover, the opportunity to work remotely contributed to their migration decision because it reduced their dependence on their pre-COVID residence and journey to work. Srygley ([2023]( "Srygley, S. \(2023\). In the nest: Did the pandemic push young adults to love with their parents? Population Reference Bureau.")) found that the share of young adults living with their parents increased at the start of COVID, but not when comparing the full three-years between 2020 and 2022 with the pre-pandemic levels. According to Kan et al., ([2024]( "Kan, U., McLeod, J., & Lopez, E. \(2024\). Non-coresident family as a driver of migration change in a crisis: The case of the COVID 19 pandemic. Humanities and Science Communications. Advance online publication.

Another important change happening to families is related to the household economic condition. Although the government has provided economic assistance to low‐ and middle‐income families, many people have lost jobs or income during the pandemic (Coibion et al., [2020]()). Worse economic conditions make people question their ability to move. The economic losses and unemployment since the pandemic could render families less motivated to move even though they are unsatisfied with their current living conditions. On the other hand, economic shocks and unemployment can sometimes force people to move because they cannot afford existing housing. Fortunately, the Coronavirus Aid, Relief and Economic Security Act, the Emergency Rental Assistance (ERA) programme, the forbearance plan and the nationwide halt on evictions have helped families bear their current housing expenses and improve housing stability. These assistance programmes should have prevented many involuntary moves (i.e., evictions) and reduced intentions to move due to economic difficulties. Thus, we expect that the general economic downturn coupled with these assistance plans are counterforces that reduce the overall volume of residential mobility during the pandemic.

In addition, families and social ties outside of the households also affect the residential moves by shaping people's needs to move and reshaping their preferences about location (Gillespie & Mulder, [2020](); Spring et al., [2017]()). Data from the Current Population Survey show that among people who moved between 2012 and 2013, 48% reported their main reason for moving to be housing‐related, approximately 30% said they moved mainly for family‐related reasons and fewer than 20% reported employment as their main reason (Ihrke, [2014]()). Researchers also found that the location of siblings, parents and friends can affect whether and where individuals move (Gillespie et al., [2022](); Mulder et al., [2020]()). COVID‐19 has taken a toll on individual physical and mental health and burdened the healthcare system. We expect that more individuals have had family members outside of the household who faced health problems and needed care during the pandemic than before. Thus, more individuals needed to move to receive care from or provide care to family members. A study in Spain during the pandemic suggests that 46% of movers cited the need to be near and care for loved ones as the reason for moving (Duque‐Calvache et al., [2020]()). Media stories documented that people started to consider moving older parents out of assisted living facilities or nursing homes due to the high risk of contracting COVID‐19 in these facilities and the loneliness caused by social distancing (Graham, [2020]()). Moreover, given the loneliness and mental stress due to social distancing, people may consider moving closer to families during the pandemic even without family responsibilities.

What could explain these migration patterns? When gathering their moving data, [United Van Lines also asks those who are moving why they decided to relocate](). The different reasons for moving that were cited and the percentages of people who gave those reasons for relocating can be compared over our period of study of the raw moving data—namely, 2018–21. During the pre-pandemic period of 2018–19, 51.4% of the respondents to United Van Lines’ survey question about moving rationale cited a job change or transfer as their main reason for relocating, compared with 37.1% during the pandemic-era period of 2020–21. Only 23.2% of the respondents cited moving to be physically closer to family in pre-pandemic times, compared with 29.6% in pandemic times. Retirement destinations and lifestyle preferences edged up as motivations for moving among the respondents, rising from a combined 29.8% in the pre-pandemic period to 31.8% in the pandemic-era period. Covid-motivated moves, while still around 10% in the fourth quarter of 2021, were noticeably lower than their level at year-end 2020.

The findings lead us to draw a few conclusions. First, regarding the direct effect of the pandemic on mobility intentions, we found a surge in searches related to short‐term escape at the onset of the pandemic in the first week of March 2020. The people who intend to move to Hawaii or Florida may already have a vacation home there. They would like to avoid the risk of the disease and find a better environment to quarantine. As shown in a survey by Pew Research Center, among U.S. adults who moved due to the pandemic, 28% cited ‘to reduce their risk of contracting the virus’ as their main reason (Cohn, [2021]()). The increased thoughts about temporary escape are consistent with the dramatically increased temporary change‐of‐address requests sent to USPS in March and April 2020 (Bowman, [2021]()). However, in the long term, temporary relocation intentions have declined by 30%–50% due to restrictions on travel.

Third, although the pandemic dampened mobility intentions in the initial stage of the pandemic, since the summer of 2020, it increased searches related to most types of moving, including moves through purchases of houses or condos, house rental and moving in with family. The only exception is moving related to apartment rental. The long‐term increases in searches on purchase‐related and house rental‐related terms reflect a discrepancy between household needs and current residential conditions during the pandemic. For example, working and studying from home may have created demands for larger spaces and better housing conditions. A recent survey showed that the share of Americans who are satisfied with the quality of life in their local community has dropped between 2018 and 2021 (Parker et al., [2021]()). The pandemic could have also changed people's evaluation of place characteristics. Features like high population density and closeness to highways and train/bus stations may be less valued than before. Fewer U.S. adults in 2021 expressed a preference for living in urban areas than in 2018 (Parker et al., [2021]()).

Pew Research Center conducted this survey to understand how Americans’ lives are being impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic. For this analysis, we surveyed 13,200 U.S. adults from Aug. 3 to Aug. 16, 2020. Everyone who took part is a member of the Center’s American Trends Panel (ATP), an online survey panel that is recruited through national, random sampling of residential addresses. This way nearly all U.S. adults have a chance of selection. The survey is weighted to be representative of the U.S. adult population by gender, race, ethnicity, partisan affiliation, education and other categories. Read more about the [ATP’s methodology]().

Table [2]( "Link to table") presents equivalent evidence for reason-specific migration. In Panel 1, the 2020 odds of migrating were statistically significantly lower than in 2019 for employment (OR = 0.78; _p_ < 0.01), lifestyle (OR = 0.74; _p_ < 0.01), and involuntary reasons (0.72; _p_ < 0.01). The odds ratio on amenity reasons was also below one and marginally significant (0.83; _p_ < 0.1). When comparing the 2019/2020 and 2018/2019 rates of change in the odds of migrating, we observed statistically significant differences for employment (_p_ < 0.03), lifestyle (_p_ < 0.02), and involuntary (_p_ < 0.04) reasons and marginally significant differences for amenity (_p_ < 0.1) and family (_p_ < 0.1) reasons. Using an alternative specification, Panel 2 in Table [2]( "Link to table") confirms the decreases in for the odds of migrating for employment (OR = 0.78; _p_ < 0.01), amenity (OR = 0.85; _p_ < 0.05), lifestyle (OR = 0.75; _p_ < 0.01), and involuntary (OR = 0.76; _p_ < 0.01) reasons. Focusing on the reasons that exhibit statistically significant results for all three tests, we conclude that employment and involuntary migration have declined following the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. The decline in employment-related migration aligns with observations in other developed countries (Haslag & Weagley, [2021]()), and could be explained by a shift to reworking coupled with server lockdowns in 2020. Perhaps more surprising is the decrease in migration due to involuntary reasons, which might result from eviction moratoria for renters put in place for 6 months from April 2020.

Following the coronavirus outbreak, a sizable share of Americans relocated for a variety of pandemic-related reasons. This research sought to trace how the dynamics behind decisions to move changed over time. To do so, 12,648 U.S. adults were surveyed from Nov. 18-29, 2020, and the results were compared with those from a survey conducted June 4-10, 2020. Everyone who took part is a member of Pew Research Center’s American Trends Panel (ATP), an online survey panel that is recruited through national, random sampling of residential addresses. This way nearly all U.S. adults have a chance of selection. The survey is weighted to be representative of the U.S. adult population by gender, race, ethnicity, partisan affiliation, education and other categories. Read more about the [ATP’s methodology]().

Survey respondents were recruited from four nationally representative sources: Pew Research Center’s American Trends Panel (conducted online), NORC’s AmeriSpeak panel (conducted online or by phone), Ipsos’ KnowledgePanel (conducted online) and a national cross-sectional survey by Pew Research Center (conducted online and by mail). Responses were collected from Nov. 19, 2019, to June 3, 2020, but most respondents completed the survey between Jan. 21 and Feb. 10, 2020. For more information, see the [Methodology]() for this report. The exact wording of the questions used in this analysis can be found here.

# The Impact of the Early Pandemic on American Mobility and the Pew Research Center Surveys

The onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020 triggered a notable shift in American mobility patterns, as millions of individuals made the difficult decision to leave their homes. These moves were often driven by immediate health concerns, particularly the fear of infection, and the abrupt closure of college campuses, which prompted many students to return to their families' residences. In the first few months of the year, slightly more than 3 percent of the adult American population relocated due to the pandemic, while an additional 8.5 percent moved for reasons unrelated to the crisis, resulting in a total migration rate of 11.6 percent among respondents in Wave 68 of the Pew Research Center’s American Trends Panel (ATP) [citation:txt1]. This migration rate was notably higher than the annual migration rate reported by the Current Population Survey (CPS) in 2020, which stood at slightly less than 9 percent [citation:txt1].

To better understand the evolving nature of these pandemic-induced relocations, the Pew Research Center conducted two major surveys in 2020. The first survey was fielded in June 2020, and the second in November of the same year, offering a longitudinal view of how motivations and destinations for moving shifted as the pandemic progressed [citation:txt12]. These surveys were part of the ATP, a nationally representative online panel recruited through a random sampling of residential addresses, ensuring that nearly all U.S. adults had an equal chance of being selected. The data collected was weighted to reflect the U.S. adult population accurately by gender, race, ethnicity, partisan affiliation, education, and other demographic categories [citation:txt12].

The Pew Research Center's methodology also included clear definitions for income tiers to facilitate more nuanced analysis. "Middle income," "lower income," and "upper income" were determined based on adjusted median family income, allowing researchers to examine how different socioeconomic groups were affected by the pandemic’s migration trends [citation:txt1]. Additionally, it is important to note that the survey's Asian American sample included only English speakers and may not fully represent the broader and diverse Asian American population [citation:txt18].

By examining these early patterns of movement and the motivations behind them, the Pew Research Center aimed to provide a comprehensive picture of how the pandemic reshaped American mobility and the factors that influenced it.

# Prevalence and Demographic Breakdown of Pandemic-Related Moves

As the pandemic progressed, the prevalence of pandemic-related moves among Americans increased, with distinct demographic patterns emerging between June and November 2020. According to the Pew Research Center’s surveys, 3% of U.S. adults reported moving due to the pandemic in June 2020, but this figure rose to 5% by November 2020. In total, 10% of adults in November said they had either moved themselves or had someone move in with them due to the outbreak, marking a slight increase from 8% in June [citation:txt19].

This shift in movement rates highlights the evolving nature of pandemic-related relocations, which were initially driven by immediate health concerns and later influenced by broader social and economic factors. Notably, young adults (ages 18–29) were the most likely demographic group to move due to the pandemic, with 11% reporting such a move in November. This age group’s high mobility can be attributed to factors such as college closures, remote work opportunities, and the desire to live with family or partners [citation:txt19].

In addition to age, income and race/ethnicity also played a significant role in determining who was more likely to move during the pandemic. Lower-income adults (9%) were more likely to move than middle- or upper-income adults (4%), reflecting the economic pressures and instability faced by those with limited financial resources. Similarly, Hispanic (9%) and Black (7%) adults were more likely to relocate than White adults (4%), indicating disparities in how different racial and ethnic groups navigated the challenges of the pandemic [citation:txt19].

These findings are supported by broader data on migration patterns during the early months of the pandemic. According to the National Association of Realtors, 8.95 million people moved residences between March and October 2020, slightly higher than the 8.82 million who moved during the same period in 2019. The increase in migration during the early months of the pandemic, particularly in March and April, was likely driven by pandemic-related considerations rather than pre-existing migration trends [citation:txt1].

To further illustrate the demographic breakdown of pandemic-related moves, consider the following data from the Pew Research Center. In November 2020, young adults (18–29) were the most likely to have moved due to the pandemic, at 11%, while those aged 65 and older had the lowest rate of movement at 2%. In terms of race and ethnicity, Hispanic adults had the highest rate of pandemic-related moves at 9%, followed by Asian adults at 6% and Black adults at 7%. These disparities underscore the uneven impact of the pandemic on different demographic groups, particularly in terms of access to resources and the ability to relocate [citation:txt7].

![](citation:img7)

This chart visually reinforces the data, showing that young adults and minority groups were disproportionately affected by the need to move during the pandemic. The higher mobility among these groups may have been driven by a combination of factors, including financial hardship, the need to be closer to family, and the closure of educational institutions [citation:txt19].

In summary, the data from June and November 2020 reveals a clear increase in pandemic-related moves, with young adults, lower-income individuals, and minority groups being the most affected. These findings set the stage for a deeper exploration of the reasons behind these moves and how they influenced where Americans chose to relocate.

# Evolving Reasons for Pandemic-Related Moves: A Shift Toward Financial Pressures

As the pandemic progressed, the motivations behind Americans’ decisions to move shifted significantly, reflecting the evolving challenges brought on by the crisis. In June 2020, the primary reasons for pandemic-related relocations were largely health- and education-related. For instance, 28% of respondents cited a desire to reduce their risk of contracting the virus, while 23% moved due to the closure of their college campuses or the shift to online learning [citation:txt11]. However, by November 2020, financial concerns had become the dominant reason, with 32% of movers citing job loss or other financial problems—up from 18% in June [citation:txt1]. This marked a notable transition from initial pandemic fears to the long-term economic consequences of the crisis.

The increasing emphasis on financial pressures was not the only change; the relative importance of other motivations also shifted. For example, the share of Americans who moved to be closer to family or a partner decreased from 20% in June to 17% in November [citation:txt1]. Similarly, the percentage of those who moved due to the perceived risk of living in areas with high infection rates dropped from 28% to 14%. College closures and local restrictions also saw declines, from 23% to 14% and from 12%, respectively [citation:txt1]. These changes suggest that as the pandemic continued, the immediate health-related anxieties that initially drove relocations gave way to more practical concerns, particularly around employment and financial stability.

Financial pressures not only influenced those who moved but also affected those who had someone move in with them. By November 2020, 36% of individuals who had a new housemate cited financial problems as the main reason for the move [citation:txt1]. This underscores how economic hardship was reshaping household structures and living arrangements across the country. The growing reliance on shared housing as a financial coping strategy was a clear indicator of the broader economic strain many Americans faced during the pandemic.

The data also reveals that while financial concerns became more prevalent, they did not completely overshadow other motivations. The desire to be near family or a partner remained a significant reason, suggesting that social and emotional needs continued to play a role in relocation decisions. Additionally, a small but notable portion of Americans still moved to avoid areas with high infection rates or to escape strict local restrictions. However, these reasons became less dominant as time passed, reinforcing the idea that the pandemic's economic fallout was increasingly shaping mobility patterns.

The shift in motivations is further illustrated in the accompanying bar chart, which compares the percentage of respondents who cited various reasons for moving in June and November 2020. As shown, financial reasons saw the most substantial increase, rising from 18% to 33%, while health-related and educational concerns declined sharply [citation:img1]. This visual representation highlights the trajectory of pandemic-induced migration and the growing role of economic hardship in influencing relocation decisions.

In the next section, we will explore how these evolving reasons for moving influenced the destinations and living arrangements of pandemic-era migrants, and how different demographic groups experienced the impact of their relocations.

# Changes in Destinations and Living Arrangements of Pandemic Movers

As the pandemic progressed, the destinations and living arrangements of those who relocated due to the crisis underwent notable shifts. In June 2020, a significant majority of pandemic-related movers—61%—chose to move in with family members, likely driven by a combination of health concerns, the closure of colleges, and early economic uncertainty [citation:txt10]. However, by November 2020, this share had dropped to 42%, indicating a change in priorities or circumstances among Americans [citation:txt1]. This decline may reflect the increasing normalization of the pandemic, a reduced sense of urgency to seek shelter with relatives, or a shift in economic conditions that made independent housing more feasible or necessary.

Conversely, the percentage of movers who rented or purchased a new home increased from 9% in June to 16% in November [citation:txt1]. This trend could be attributed to the growing feasibility of remote work, which reduced the need to live near traditional urban centers, and the availability of government assistance programs that provided temporary financial relief and helped stabilize housing markets [citation:txt2]. In addition, 10% of pandemic movers relocated to a vacation home by November, and 8% moved in with a friend, suggesting a diverse set of motivations and living preferences [citation:txt7].

The shift in living arrangements also reveals patterns in who moved in with whom. Among those who hosted someone due to the pandemic, 51% reported that it was an adult child or child’s spouse, while 23% said it was a parent or parent-in-law. Other common arrangements included friends (29%) and romantic partners (24%), with the remaining cases involving other relationships [citation:txt12]. These patterns highlight the central role of family in pandemic-era housing decisions and the broader societal trend of young adults returning to live with their parents. In fact, by July 2020, a majority of young adults were living with their parents, a phenomenon not seen since the Great Depression [citation:txt10].

The evolving nature of these living arrangements also reflects broader economic and social shifts. As the pandemic continued, financial pressures became a more prominent factor in relocation decisions, with fewer people citing the immediate health risks of the virus as their primary motivation [citation:txt2]. This financial shift likely influenced the decline in family-based relocations and the rise in independent housing solutions, as individuals sought to balance cost, safety, and long-term stability [citation:txt2].

These changes in destinations and living arrangements during the pandemic also had lasting implications. For example, about 58% of those who had people move in with them due to the pandemic reported that at least one of them was still there by the end of 2020, suggesting that some pandemic-era living arrangements had transitioned from temporary to more permanent solutions [citation:txt1]. At the same time, 39% of people who had someone move in with them no longer had anyone living with them due to the pandemic, indicating that some relocations were indeed temporary [citation:txt1].

The visual representation of these shifts further illustrates the changing landscape of pandemic-related relocations. A bar chart comparing June and November 2020 data shows a clear decline in the percentage of people moving in with family and a corresponding increase in independent housing options [citation:img1]. This trend underscores the dynamic nature of the pandemic’s impact on American living arrangements and highlights the resilience and adaptability of individuals and families during a period of unprecedented uncertainty.

In the following section, we will examine the demographic groups most affected by these changes in living arrangements and how individuals perceived the impact of their relocations on their overall well-being.

# The Permanence of Pandemic-Related Moves and Living Arrangements

As the pandemic continued to shape the American landscape, the permanence of pandemic-related relocations became a key area of interest. According to the Pew Research Center’s November 2020 survey, 69% of individuals who had moved due to the pandemic were still living in a different home at that time. This group was composed of 40% who had settled in a new community and 29% who had found a new home within their original community. In contrast, 31% of pandemic movers had returned to their pre-pandemic residences by November 2020, indicating a significant but not overwhelming trend of returning to prior living situations [citation:txt3].

The decision to remain in a new location or return was influenced by a variety of factors, including the reasons for the initial move, financial stability, and personal circumstances. Those who relocated due to financial pressures or health-related concerns were more likely to remain in their new homes, as these motivations often reflected deeper, longer-term shifts in lifestyle and economic conditions [citation:txt11].

In addition to examining where pandemic movers ended up, researchers also looked at the lasting impact of shared living arrangements. The Pew Research Center found that 58% of individuals who had taken in someone during the pandemic still had at least one person living with them as of November 2020. Meanwhile, 39% had no additional housemates remaining. These figures underscore the complex and often temporary nature of pandemic-induced household changes, as many people moved in together out of necessity but later moved out as circumstances improved [citation:txt3].

The persistence of new living arrangements, both in terms of relocation and shared housing, reflected broader societal shifts. For example, the increase in remote work and the decline in urban density due to the pandemic led to a reevaluation of where and how people chose to live. Some individuals moved to more affordable areas or into shared housing as a way to cope with economic uncertainty, while others sought out new communities that offered better access to resources or a better quality of life [citation:txt17].

These trends were not uniform across all demographic groups. Younger adults, for instance, were more likely to move in with family or friends during the pandemic and often remained in those arrangements for extended periods. Similarly, individuals with lower incomes were more likely to experience temporary or permanent housing changes due to financial instability [citation:txt13].

The data from the Pew Research Center surveys highlights the fact that many pandemic-related moves were not temporary disruptions but rather significant, long-term shifts in the American housing landscape. As the pandemic’s impact continues to unfold, the question of how many of these changes will persist remains an open one, with implications for urban development, housing policy, and the future of American mobility.

# Perceived Outcomes of Pandemic-Related Moves Versus Other Moves

The relocation decisions made by Americans during the pandemic were often shaped by urgent and uncertain circumstances, and these differences are reflected in the perceptions of the move’s impact. According to the Pew Research Center’s November 2020 survey, only 43% of individuals who moved due to the pandemic reported that their relocation had a positive impact on their lives, compared to 61% of those who moved for other reasons. In contrast, 29% of pandemic movers described the impact of their move as negative, compared to just 12% of those who moved for other reasons. These findings underscore the complex and often challenging nature of pandemic-related relocations, which were frequently driven by factors such as health concerns, job loss, or the need to live closer to family rather than by personal choice or long-term planning [citation:txt19].

One possible explanation for the lower rates of positive perception among pandemic movers is the abrupt and often involuntary nature of their relocations. Many individuals were forced to move due to financial hardship, health risks, or changes in work and education environments, which may have made the transition more stressful and less satisfying. In contrast, those who moved for other reasons—such as career opportunities, personal preferences, or lifestyle changes—may have had greater control over their decisions and were more likely to view the move as a positive step forward [citation:txt10].

The data also reveals that a larger proportion of pandemic movers (28%) described the impact of their move as “neither positive nor negative,” compared to 25% of other movers. This suggests that for a significant share of pandemic-related relocations, the experience may have been neutral or mixed, without a clear positive or negative outcome. This could reflect the uncertainty and instability of the pandemic period, during which many people were still adjusting to their new living situations and assessing the long-term implications of their moves [citation:txt19].

The differences in perceived outcomes between the two groups also highlight the broader socioeconomic and psychological toll of the pandemic. As noted in previous sections, financial pressures became a more prominent factor in relocation decisions over time, and many pandemic movers faced significant economic challenges that may have limited their ability to achieve a positive outcome from their move [citation:txt6]. Additionally, the stress and uncertainty associated with the pandemic likely contributed to higher rates of dissatisfaction and negative perceptions among those who relocated during this period [citation:txt9].

As the country continues to recover from the pandemic, it remains to be seen how these experiences will shape future migration trends and housing preferences [citation:txt6].
